entries.notes: Virginia regulations permit Tier II generators to operate only in emergencies, generally defined as sudden and reasonably unforeseeable events including power outages or natural disasters. Tier IV generators may run outside emergencies but carry more costly emission controls. The guidance adds a utility-scheduled planned outage to the emergency definition, using a scenario in which notice is provided within 14 days or less. A stated driver is that over 100 planned transmission upgrades require temporary outages for grid users.

entries.instrument: Virginia DEQ consent order, Microsoft Leesburg data center
entries.summary: DEQ ordered approximately $2.5 million after a Leesburg data center exceeded its air permit running backup generators during a four-day substation outage. Reported as the agency's largest civil penalty.

source.citation: WJLA and regional reporting, September 16 2026, citing state documents and a DEQ spokesperson

entries.notes: Facility at 19515 Compass Creek Parkway, Leesburg. Outage at the Cochran Mill Electrical Substation June 27 to July 1, 2025. DEQ calculated that for the rolling year October 4, 2024 to October 3, 2025 the facility emitted approximately 102 tons NOx against a 94.67 ton limit, 5.158 tons particulate matter against 3.34, and 11.599 tons VOC against 6.86, all on a rolling 365-day average. Fuel throughput approximately 1,190,000 gallons against a permit limit of 665,850 gallons. Microsoft states its emissions calculation method was less accurate and that it invested approximately $31 million in a system to prevent a future extended outage.
entries.confidence_note: The consent order itself has not been read. Not final: public comment runs through October 14, 2026 before it can be finalized. All figures are attributed to a DEQ spokesperson through a news outlet, not taken from the order. No inference is drawn about whether the exceedance was avoidable.

entries.instrument: Virginia air permit structure for data center backup generators
entries.summary: Backup generator permits are written as annual emissions tonnage and fuel throughput on a rolling 365-day average, not as hours of operation. Reporting states that so long as a generator stays under its permitted annual level there is no limit on how much it runs.

source.citation: Virginia Mercury, January 14 2026, on Tier II generator permitting

entries.notes: Bears directly on how an exceedance occurs. A single extended outage can consume a substantial share of an annual allowance without any hourly limit being broken. In the Leesburg consent order the reported fuel throughput was approximately 1,190,000 gallons against a permit limit of 665,850, arising from a four-day outage.
entries.confidence_note: No permit has been read. The structure is described from reporting on Virginia's regime and may not generalize to other states. Whether any hours-based condition also applies is NOT_CHECKED.

entries.summary: Requires data centers applying for air permits on or after July 1, 2026 to meet emissions limits at least as stringent as a stated standard, with DEQ guidance pointing toward Tier 4 controls.

source.citation: Data Center Knowledge, July 2026, on revised Virginia DEQ generator rules

entries.notes: Associated DEQ guidance applies to permit applications submitted on or after July 1, 2026 and reflects a stated conclusion that hyperscale backup fleets no longer fit traditional emergency-only assumptions. Reported control technologies include selective catalytic reduction, diesel particulate filters, and continuous emissions monitoring systems.

entries.summary: Loudoun County Attorney Leo Rogers is reported to have stated that a moratorium is not allowed in the Commonwealth of Virginia, but that a pause on legislative applications is allowed.

source.citation: DC News Now, September 16 2026

entries.notes: Legislative applications are the discretionary ones, rezonings and special exceptions, as distinct from by-right or administrative review. The distinction appears to be the drafting theory behind the Loudoun pause. A neighboring Virginia city separately distinguishes a pause pending ordinance revision from a moratorium, described there as a total wipeout of one specific use.

entries.summary: Proposes an Interim Resource Adequacy Service applying to new large loads that have not brought their own new capacity, under which utilities would be notified to reduce or transfer demand from those loads before any action affecting traditional consumers during low-supply conditions.

source.citation: Virginia Mercury, August 27 2026, and regional reporting

entries.notes: Covers a thirteen-state footprint including Ohio and Virginia. PJM requested a FERC decision within 60 days of filing. The filing rests on a Ratepayer Protection Pledge introduced in March 2026 and expanded in July under which new large loads build, bring or buy the generation needed to satisfy their demand and pay its full cost. The filing also proposes a registry of all large loads of at least 50 MW by site, service area, and whether they bring their own supply.
